problem: VLM-based VLN navigators supervise progress tracking and local execution jointly via next-action prediction, so semantic-progress errors (wrong active sub-instruction) cannot be told apart from execution errors. DAgger-style relabeling of off-path states fixes the next motion but never corrects the progress state.
motivation: Progress must be grounded in the global instruction and long visual history, whereas execution depends on recent observations. Once an agent leaves the demonstrated route, a corrective action label does not say whether the wrong step is active or the right step is executed poorly, so the agent keeps deciding from an erroneous progress state. Making progress an explicit interface allows supervision to be assigned to the level it should improve.
key_idea: Split VLN into an Instruction Analysis module that predicts the active sub-instruction and execution state (Normal/Recovering) and an Action Generation module conditioned on that interface, with state-level supervision from geometry-grounded rollouts and expert-action supervision only for persistent execution failures.
insight: State-level correction, action-level correction and DAgger each give only small gains alone (SR 50.6, 49.4, 49.8 vs 48.1 for expert-only). Combining 190K state samples with just 11.5K selective action labels reaches 55.3 SR, beating 190K state + 200K conventional action labels (54.4), so where supervision is placed matters more than how much. State correction raises deviated-history sub-instruction accuracy (FG-R2R 43.54→54.05) without changing on-path accuracy. A unified 7B model trained on the same data only reaches 50.7 SR, so the explicit inference-time interface, not the progress supervision alone, drives the gain. The predicted sub-instruction also helps four frozen policies.
method: Semantic–Execution Interface: M_IA(I, V_1:t) -> (s_t, m_t) gives the active sub-instruction and execution state; M_AG(I, s_t, m_t, V_{t-k:t}) predicts action chunks of up to 3 primitives from a short recent window; the two are trained independently with no gradient across the interface.

E-SPA alignment: an LLM (qwen3-vl-flash) rewrites each R2R instruction into ordered executable sub-instructions. Dynamic programming then partitions the expert trajectory into contiguous segments, minimizing CLIP visual-text cost, action-intent consistency cost (weights 0.4/0.6), a duration regularizer, and a stair-height hard anchor. Segment-end poses become semantic waypoints (position + heading).
RxR / FG-R2R mapping: Landmark-RxR annotations are projected onto RxR-CE trajectories for training; human FG-R2R alignments are projected onto R2R-CE but used only for evaluating M_IA.

Fixed-sub-instruction rollouts: with s_k fixed, M_AG is sampled several times at temperature 0.5. If all fail to reach the waypoint (1.5 m / 45°), one expert-intervention rollout is added, with the expert taking over on deviation and handing control back on reconnection. Expert-guided segments are labeled Recovering, others Normal.

Level-separated supervision: all rollout histories give state targets (s_t, m_t) to M_IA, with the sub-instruction held until the waypoint is reached physically. Only Recovering intervals of failed groups give expert action chunks to M_AG (11.5K samples).

Two-stage training: expert-path initialization (~200K M_IA and 650K M_AG samples from R2R+RxR, lr 1e-5), then mixed expert and corrective training (lr 5e-6). Both are Qwen2.5-VL-3B SFT with a frozen ViT.
Plug-and-play transfer: M_IA's predicted sub-instruction is appended as 'Current Sub-instruction: ...' to the text input of frozen policies with no retraining.

setting.backbone: Two Qwen2.5-VL-3B models (M_IA and M_AG), SFT-finetuned; E-SPA preprocessing uses qwen3-vl-flash/plus and CLIP ViT-L/14
setting.training_data: R2R-CE and RxR-CE expert trajectories (~200K M_IA and 650K M_AG samples), Landmark-RxR alignments, E-SPA-derived R2R sub-instruction alignments, plus ~190K state-level and 11.5K action-level rollout samples. No extra navigation or VL data.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB 640x480, 79° HFOV; history up to 16 frames for M_IA, 8 frames from the latest 40 for M_AG
setting.action_space: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 15° / STOP, predicted in chunks of up to 3
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT alignments, waypoints and expert used only in training; FG-R2R only for M_IA evaluation)

numbers.extra: 190K state-level + 11.5K action-level corrective samples; no extra nav/VL data; 500-step limit, 3 m success radius
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Comparison on R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen), Route2Step row

numbers.eval_set_note: 3,570 of 3,669 episodes; 99 episodes in scene oLBMNvg9in8 excluded for all methods because geodesic distance is infinite
numbers.extra: same corrective budget as R2R-CE; Landmark-RxR alignments used for training
numbers.evidence: Table 1, Route2Step row; Appendix C.1 on the excluded episodes

numbers.extra: trained on complete expert + corrective data, no explicit interface at inference
numbers.evidence: Text: 'this baseline achieves 50.7% SR and 44.1% SPL'

numbers_note: Real-world results (19/33 trials; 3/5 vs 0/5 for StreamVLN indoors) are counts, not standard benchmark metrics, so are not listed. Plug-in transfer results (e.g. StreamVLN 56.8/50.5 → 57.4/52.3) are for other policies with M_IA injected.
results: Route2Step reaches 55.3 SR / 48.2 SPL on R2R-CE val-unseen, up from 48.1/43.3 for expert-only training, and 54.8 SR / 42.6 SPL on RxR-CE, without extra nav or VL data. It beats a unified 7B baseline (50.7/44.1) and, with the same state correction, 200K conventional DAgger labels (54.4/46.7). Progress-Think has higher R2R-CE SR/SPL (60.1/53.6) and ETPNav/HNR are stronger, though they use RL, panoramas or other setups.
limitations: Gains rely on E-SPA alignments built from LLM sub-instruction rewriting and CLIP, so alignment errors propagate into supervision; the alignment quality is not evaluated directly.
Route2Step does not lead R2R-CE and trails on RxR-CE SPL/nDTW versus several baselines (e.g., DecoVLN, ETPNav, HNR); baseline counts are not comparable.
Real-world evaluation is small (33 trials, 19 successes) and the controlled comparison is a single task with 5 trials; two-model inference runs on a remote GPU.
